historical_record.description: Floyd Jennings built a camera obscura on the terrace below the Cliff House, facing the sea: a 17.5-foot square redwood-sided room with a rotating hood on the roof holding a mirror and a lens of 150-inch focal length, which cast a moving panorama of Seal Rocks, Ocean Beach and the Marin coast onto a six-foot white parabolic table. The table, lens and mirror are unchanged since. It was the first of the three Jennings built, and the second camera obscura on the site after the one on the fourth floor of Sutro's Cliff House, lost in the 1907 fire.
Life magazine ran a picture feature on the camera obscura below the Cliff House, which Floyd Jennings called his giant camera.

The camera obscura's housing was re-dressed as a giant camera at the suggestion of George K. Whitney, the Cliff House's owner: plywood sheathing over the redwood, false walls five feet wider on the north and south, two wooden knobs on the front like a film advance, and a smooth drum around the lens housing. The interior was not touched.
The camera obscura's original rotating hood over the lens and mirror was replaced with a copper-sheathed pyramid.

The Camera Obscura was listed on the National Register of Historic Places as a rare working camera obscura more than fifty years old on its original site — one of two in California, and apparently the last in the United States of that age in a building of its own.
